title: Introduction to Cryptography
subtitle: Goals of cryptography: confidentiality, integrity, authenticity

whyItExists.problem: Digital information can be read, copied, or altered by anyone with network access. Without protection, passwords, financial data, and messages travel in the open.
whyItExists.solution: Cryptography uses mathematics to transform data so only authorised parties can read it, detect tampering, and prove identity — without requiring a physical secure channel.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Whenever you store or transmit sensitive data: passwords, PII, API tokens, financial records, or private messages.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Cryptography does not protect against bugs in your application logic, misconfigured servers, or social engineering attacks.

explainModes.beginner: Cryptography is like putting a letter in a lockbox — only the person with the right key can open it and read it.
explainModes.simple: It uses math to scramble data (encryption) or prove it hasn't changed (hashing) so attackers who intercept it see only gibberish.
explainModes.standard: Cryptography provides four guarantees: confidentiality (data readable only by intended parties), integrity (tampering is detected), authentication (identity is verified), and non-repudiation (senders cannot deny actions).
explainModes.technical: Modern cryptography relies on computationally hard problems: integer factorisation (RSA), discrete logarithm (DH/ECDH), and preimage resistance (hashing). Security depends on key secrecy, not algorithm secrecy (Kerckhoffs's principle).
explainModes.deepDive: Cryptographic primitives are composed into schemes and protocols. A cipher provides confidentiality; a MAC provides integrity; combining them (AEAD) provides both. TLS is a protocol that orchestrates key exchange, authentication, and symmetric encryption using these primitives. The security proofs are in the random oracle model or standard model depending on the primitive.

content.text: Cryptography provides four core security properties. Confidentiality ensures data is readable only by authorised parties. Integrity ensures data has not been modified. Authentication verifies identity. Non-repudiation means a sender cannot later deny having sent a message.

items: Confidentiality — data is kept secret from unauthorised readers
Integrity — any modification of data is detectable
Authentication — parties can prove their identity
Non-repudiation — a signed action cannot be denied

content.definition: The original, readable data before encryption. Also called cleartext.
The encrypted, unreadable form produced by an encryption algorithm. Looks like random bytes to an attacker.
A secret value used by a cryptographic algorithm. All security rests on the key — the algorithm itself is public knowledge (Kerckhoffs's principle).
The mathematical procedure for encryption/decryption. Good algorithms are public, peer-reviewed, and standardised (e.g. AES, ChaCha20, RSA).

content.text: The simplest operation is hashing: a one-way function that turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint. Even a one-character change produces a completely different hash.

content.code:
import hashlib
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

# --- Hashing: one-way fingerprint ---
msg = b"Hello, cryptography!"
hash_val = hashlib.sha256(msg).hexdigest()
print("SHA-256:", hash_val)
# 185f8db32921bd46d35... (always the same for the same input)

# --- Symmetric encryption: reversible with a key ---
key   = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)   # random 256-bit key
nonce = os.urandom(12)                          # random 96-bit nonce
aesgcm = AESGCM(key)

ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, msg, None)
plaintext  = aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, ciphertext, None)

print("Ciphertext (hex):", ciphertext.hex())
print("Decrypted:", plaintext)   # b'Hello, cryptography!'

content.text: Kerckhoffs's principle: a cryptographic system must be secure even if everything about it except the key is public. Never rely on 'security by obscurity'.

a.name: Hashing
weaknesses: Not suitable for secrets you need to retrieve
a.useWhen: Verifying file integrity, storing passwords, digital signatures

b.name: Encryption
b.description: Two-way transformation — reversible with the correct key
strengths: Protects data in transit and at rest
b.useWhen: Storing secrets you need to retrieve (API keys, messages, files)

content.text: Never invent your own cryptographic algorithm. Home-grown crypto is almost always broken. Use standardised algorithms (AES, ChaCha20, SHA-256, RSA, ECDSA) from audited libraries.

Real-world security stacks layers of primitives. A primitive (AES, SHA-256) is a building block. A scheme (AES-GCM) combines primitives safely. A protocol (TLS) orchestrates multiple schemes to solve a full security problem.
Python's cryptography library (pyca/cryptography) is the recommended choice. Install with: pip install cryptography argon2-cffi pyjwt.

questions.question: What does confidentiality mean in cryptography?
options: Data cannot be modified without detection
Only authorised parties can read the data
Identities of communicating parties can be verified
Actions cannot be denied after the fact
questions.explanation: Confidentiality ensures data is accessible only to those authorised to read it — the classic 'keep it secret' goal.

questions.question: According to Kerckhoffs's principle, which part of a cryptosystem must be kept secret?
questions.explanation: Kerckhoffs's principle states that a system should remain secure even if everything except the key is public knowledge.

questions.question: Which cryptographic property ensures a sender cannot deny having sent a message?
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation, typically provided by digital signatures, means the sender cannot later deny having signed the message.

faq.q: Is keeping the algorithm secret a good idea?
faq.a: No. Per Kerckhoffs's principle, security must rest on the key, not the algorithm. Secret algorithms are hard to audit and historically break once discovered.

faq.q: Can I write my own encryption algorithm?
faq.a: Only for learning. Production systems must use standardised, peer-reviewed algorithms. Creating secure cryptography requires years of cryptanalysis.

faq.q: What is the difference between encoding and encryption?
faq.a: Encoding (Base64, URL encoding) transforms data for transport — it provides zero security. Encryption requires a key and provides confidentiality. Never confuse the two.

examples: Every HTTPS request uses TLS to protect data in transit
Signal Protocol uses end-to-end encryption so even Signal cannot read your messages
Git uses SHA-1 (now migrating to SHA-256) to verify commit integrity
